Welcome! I am a versatile Research Engineer/Scientist with a solid background in electronics, embedded systems, and software/hardware integration. My work focuses on applying AI and biosensing to develop scalable wearable health monitoring systems. I am always exploring innovative ways to translate technological advances into meaningful healthcare impact.

# Short Bio

Fluent in multiple human and programming languages, I hold an M.S. in Computer Science from the University of Massachusetts Lowell, an M.Eng. in Computer Engineering, and a B.S. in Electrical and Electronics Engineering from INELEC.
I am now a Ph.D. Candidate and Research Assistant at UMass Lowell’s [Miner School of Computer and Information Sciences](https://www.uml.edu/sciences/computer-science/). Before starting my PhD, I worked as an Embedded Software Engineer and was co-founder of Deadline Store and BNBE Technologies

# Brief Summary on My Research 

my research focuses on understanding biomedical phenomenon, what biomarker help us identify differences in multiple states/classes/disease; and use ai identify patterns. Understanding biomedical concepts, biomarkers, identify patterns and then develop device or interface with appropriate sensors for health monitoring and health diagnosis.

My work spans from data collection, designing device, sensor integration , wearable to collect specific biomarker, to analyzing data, curve fitting, pattern recognition , ai development, to real time deployment.

# Entrepreneurship & Business Ventures

<center>
![Hex stickers for R packages and courses I've developed](images/hex/hex_logos.png){width=80% .external}
</center>

I use and contribute to [{{< fa brands r-project >}}](https://www.r-project.org/about.html) in most of my research and teaching. One specific category of research is choice modeling. I use [choice-based conjoint](https://sawtoothsoftware.com/help/lighthouse-studio/manual/hid_web_whatcbc.html) surveys to measure people's preferences for a variety of technologies and policies. I have developed several packages for implementing conjoint in {{< fa brands r-project >}}, including [`{logitr}`](https://jhelvy.github.io/logitr/) for estimating multinomial and mixed logit models with preference space and "willingness-to-pay" space utility parameterizations, and [`{cbcTools}`](https://jhelvy.github.io/cbcTools/) for  designing and conducting power analyses for choice-based conjoint surveys. I also developed the [`{surveydown}`](https://surveydown.org/) package along with [Pingfan Hu](https://pingfanhu.com/) and Bogdan Bunea for making markdown-based surveys with Quarto shiny documents. I also co-authored the [`{renderthis}`](https://jhelvy.github.io/renderthis/) package with [Garrick Aden-Buie](https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/) for rendering media (e.g., [`xaringan`](https://github.com/yihui/xaringan) slides) into multiple different formats. Finally , I also [teach](teaching.html) multiple programming and data analytics courses in {{< fa brands r-project >}}, and all of my course materials are built using {{< fa brands r-project >}}, including course websites and slides.

You can see more of my {{< fa brands r-project >}} projects and source code on my GitHub page: [https://github.com/jhelvy/](https://github.com/jhelvy/)

I began studying Chinese during my second year as an undergraduate engineering student at Virginia Tech in the fall of 2006. The next spring, I received the Horton Scholarship, which provided a unique opportunity to travel to China and complete an educational project of my own design. I traveled to Dalian in the summer of 2008 to study language and culture at Liaoning Normal University, then I moved to Shanghai in the fall to gain international engineering experience as an intern in General Electric's Advanced Wind Turbine Operations division. The project opened my eyes to the many forces that shape the adoption of emerging technologies, in particular the importance of policy and economics. After returning to the U.S., I was awarded a [Critical Language Scholarship](http://clscholarship.org/) by the U.S. Department of State to study Chinese in Harbin, China during the summer of 2009, and I have since returned to China numerous times for work or research, including an internship at the [Innovation Center for Energy and Transportation (iCET)](http://icet.org.cn/english/index.asp) and as a 2014 [East Asia Pacific Summer Institutes (EAPSI)](http://www.nsf.gov/eapsi) Fellow supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation. Today, I continue to use my language skills and experience in China while conducting interdisciplinary research in China.
